analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from collecting, keeping, or selling personal reproductive and sexual health data beyond what serving the user requires.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since its June 2025 referral with no hearing or vote; all 101 of its cosponsors are Democrats and none are Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies outside the doctor-patient system — apps, websites, data brokers, advertisers — from collecting, keeping, using, or selling information about a person's reproductive or sexual health, including period-tracking data, searches for clinics, pregnancy status, and even guesses inferred from other data. It would give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, require plain-language privacy policies, and let the Federal Trade Commission and individuals sue violators, with damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day. It would also invalidate fine-print arbitration clauses for these disputes.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses period-tracking, fertility, or wellness apps, searches for reproductive health care, buys contraception, or visits a clinic — especially people in states where abortion is restricted, whose app data, location history, or purchase records could be bought by brokers or obtained through legal process and used against them. Doctors and hospitals already covered by HIPAA medical-privacy rules are excluded, so the bill targets the large, mostly unregulated ecosystem around them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of reproductive health apps and services

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits companies from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information except as strictly necessary to provide a product or service the user asked for, and restricts which employees can see it.

Gives people enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete their data — including data inferred by algorithms and data collected from third parties — with a list of exactly which outside companies received it, at no fee, within 15 days.

Covers location information that might indicate someone tried to obtain reproductive care, pregnancy and fertility status, contraception and abortion-related purchases, and health signals like basal temperature — plus any such facts inferred from unrelated data.

Enforces the rules through the FTC and a private right of action with statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day, attorney's fees, and a ban on pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers for these cases.
Bars companies from punishing customers who exercise these rights, such as by charging them more or degrading service.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app makers that currently collect and monetize reproductive health data would lose that data stream and bear compliance costs. Broader businesses could face costs from the bill's wide definitions and from lawsuits brought under its private right of action.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app makers

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: 'regulated entity' reaches essentially any business engaged in commerce, and covered information includes anything inferred or extrapolated from non-health data, so many ordinary companies would need to audit their data practices to comply.

The private right of action with per-day statutory damages and a ban on arbitration agreements could produce substantial litigation costs, and a court — not the parties' contract — decides whether arbitration applies.
Entities covered by HIPAA are excluded, creating a two-track system in which data held by a clinic is protected one way and the same facts held by an app or search engine another way.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are strong and directly address a real gap: since the fall of Roe, reproductive health data held outside HIPAA can be sold or subpoenaed, and people in restricted states face real exposure. The costs are real but conventional for a privacy law — compliance work across many industries and a litigation regime that may be aggressive, with per-day damages. The bill preserves state laws that offer more protection, so it sets a floor rather than a ceiling. On balance, the protections outweigh the compliance and litigation costs, though the breadth of the definitions is a legitimate complaint.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the bill on June 11, 2025, joined by 60 original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over consumer privacy legislation.
As of the latest action record, the committee has held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.
The bill's support is 101 House Democrats plus its Democratic sponsor; no Republican has cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertisers, and app makers keep collecting and monetizing reproductive and sexual health data without a federal privacy rule, because the bill never left committee.

for.name: Rep. Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the My Body, My Data Act and recruited 60 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral on June 11, 2025 and has taken no action on it — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat — 101 of them — and no Republican has signed on; the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee has not moved the bill.

industries.note: These firms buy, sell, and target advertising with reproductive and sexual health signals — location near a clinic, pregnancy inferences, purchase histories — and the bill bans collecting, retaining, or selling that data except to serve the user. That data is exactly what can end up in the hands of litigants or prosecutors in states that restrict abortion.

industries.industry: Fertility, period-tracking, and sexual wellness app makers
industries.note: These apps lose the ability to monetize or share the intimate data at the core of their products and face lawsuit exposure, but they gain a uniform federal rule and their users gain protection that could rebuild trust in the category.

analysis.trajectory: With zero Republican cosponsors and no committee action eight months after referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup in the divided House this Congress; the most likely path is expiring when the 119th Congress ends, as earlier versions of this proposal have.
